name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q01 - Components and initiation of plant development

questiontext.text: Development in a flowering plant is broadly considered as the sum of which two processes, and what is the first step in the process of plant growth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The development of a mature plant from a zygote follows a precise, ordered succession of events involving both increase in size and specialisation of cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
Development is defined as the sum of two processes: growth and differentiation. The first step in the process of plant growth is seed germination, which occurs when favourable environmental conditions return and the seed resumes metabolic activities.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, development is the sum of growth and differentiation, and seed germination is the first step in plant growth.

answer.text: Growth and differentiation; seed germination
Dedifferentiation and senescence; flowering
Cell division and dormancy; fruit formation
Photoperiodism and vernalisation; secondary growth

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q02 - Definition of biological growth in plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following best defines biological growth in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biological growth is a fundamental characteristic of living beings that involves permanent structural addition driven by cellular metabolism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Growth is defined as an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts, or even an individual cell. It is accompanied by both anabolic and catabolic metabolic processes that occur at the expense of energy. Reversible physical swelling, such as a piece of wood swelling in water, is not biological growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, biological growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size accompanied by energy-expending metabolic processes.

answer.text: A reversible increase in volume due to passive water uptake
An irreversible permanent increase in size accompanied by metabolic processes at the expense of energy
A temporary increase in fresh weight without any change in protoplasm
An increase in cell size driven solely by catabolic reactions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q03 - Meristems responsible for primary and secondary growth

questiontext.text: In dicotyledonous plants and gymnosperms, which meristems appear later in life and cause an increase in the girth of the organs in which they are active?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants exhibit primary growth (elongation along the axis) and secondary growth (increase in girth).

Step 2: Evaluation
Root apical meristem and shoot apical meristem are responsible for primary growth. In dicotyledonous plants and gymnosperms, lateral meristems—specifically the vascular cambium and cork-cambium—appear later in life and cause an increase in girth, which is termed secondary growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The meristems responsible for secondary growth (increase in girth) are vascular cambium and cork-cambium.

answer.text: Root apical meristem and shoot apical meristem
Intercalary meristem and root-cap cells
Vascular cambium and cork-cambium
Shoot apical meristem and intercalary meristem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q04 - Quantitative examples of plant growth measurement

questiontext.text: Which pair correctly matches a plant system with its quantitative growth expression?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Growth is measured by parameters proportional to protoplasmic increase, such as cell number, cell size, length, and surface area.

Step 2: Evaluation
One single maize root apical meristem can give rise to more than 17,500 new cells per hour (growth expressed as increase in cell number), whereas cells in a watermelon may increase in size by up to 3,50,000 times (growth expressed as increase in cell size).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, maize root apical meristem producing more than 17,500 new cells per hour and watermelon cells increasing in size up to 3,50,000 times are the accurate quantitative expressions.

answer.text: Maize root apical meristem: cell size increases up to 17,500 times
Watermelon cells: produce more than 3,50,000 new cells per hour
Pollen tube: measured in terms of surface area
Maize root apical meristem: more than 17,500 new cells per hour

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q05 - Cellular features of meristematic growth phase

questiontext.text: Which set of characteristics accurately describes cells in the meristematic phase of growth at the root and shoot apices?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The period of growth is divided into meristematic, elongation, and maturation phases, each with distinct cellular features.

Step 2: Evaluation
Constantly dividing cells in the meristematic phase are rich in protoplasm and possess large conspicuous nuclei. Their cell walls are primary in nature, thin, and cellulosic with abundant plasmodesmatal connections. Increased vacuolation and wall thickening occur in subsequent phases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cells in the meristematic phase are rich in protoplasm, have large conspicuous nuclei, and possess thin primary cellulosic walls with abundant plasmodesmatal connections.

answer.text: Rich in protoplasm, large conspicuous nuclei, thin primary cellulosic walls with abundant plasmodesmatal connections
Increased vacuolation, thick lignocellulosic secondary walls, and loss of protoplasm
Maximal cell size, sparse plasmodesmata, and extensive protoplasmic modifications
Large central vacuole, suberised cell walls, and absence of nuclei

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q06 - Characteristics of the elongation phase of growth

questiontext.text: In a growing root tip, the cells lying just proximal (away from the tip) to the meristematic zone belong to the phase of elongation. Which features characterise these cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Immediately behind the meristematic apex lies the zone of elongation, which is responsible for the greatest longitudinal extension of the root axis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cells in the phase of elongation are characterised by increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition. Using the parallel line technique, the zones immediately behind the apex are observed to elongate the most.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition characterise the phase of elongation.

answer.text: Constant mitotic division and absence of vacuoles
Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition
Complete loss of protoplasm and cessation of wall deposition
Attainment of maximal wall thickening and final tissue differentiation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q07 - Features of cells in maturation phase

questiontext.text: Which region of the plant axis contains cells that attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Moving proximal to the phase of elongation, cells enter the final phase of growth where they achieve their permanent adult form.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the phase of maturation, which lies further away from the apex (more proximal to the phase of elongation), cells attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications. Most mature tissues and cell types represent this phase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cells attain maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications during the phase of maturation.

answer.text: Meristematic phase
Phase of elongation
Phase of maturation
Lag phase of geometrical growth

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q08 - Calculation of root length in arithmetic growth

questiontext.text: A plant root elongates at a constant arithmetic growth rate of \(0.5\text{ cm day}^{-1}\). If its initial length at time \(t = 0\) is \(2.0\text{ cm}\), what will be its length after \(8\text{ days}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial length \(L_0 = 2.0\text{ cm}\), constant growth rate \(r = 0.5\text{ cm day}^{-1}\), and time \(t = 8\text{ days}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The root follows arithmetic growth where elongation occurs at a constant rate per unit time along a linear trajectory.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Arithmetic growth is mathematically expressed as \(L_t = L_0 + rt\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting the given values into the equation:
\(L_8 = 2.0\text{ cm} + (0.5\text{ cm day}^{-1} \times 8\text{ days})\)
\(L_8 = 2.0\text{ cm} + 4.0\text{ cm} = 6.0\text{ cm}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units match (\(\text{cm}\)) and the value is greater than \(L_0\), as expected for positive elongation. The final length after \(8\text{ days}\) is \(6.0\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q09 - Efficiency index in exponential plant growth

questiontext.text: In the exponential growth equation \(W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}\), what does the parameter \(r\) represent, and how does the final size \(W_1\) relate to \(W_0\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Exponential (geometrical) growth occurs when both progeny cells after mitotic division retain the ability to divide, leading to rapid multiplication proportional to existing size.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}\), \(W_1\) is the final size, \(W_0\) is the initial size, \(t\) is time, and \(e\) is the base of natural logarithms. Here, \(r\) is the relative growth rate and serves as the measure of the plant's ability to produce new plant material, referred to as the efficiency index. Because \(W_1\) is directly proportional to \(W_0\), the final size depends on the initial size.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(r\) represents the relative growth rate (efficiency index), and the final size \(W_1\) depends directly on the initial size \(W_0\).

answer.text: \(r\) is the relative growth rate (efficiency index), and \(W_1\) depends on the initial size \(W_0\).
\(r\) is the absolute growth rate, and \(W_1\) is independent of \(W_0\).
\(r\) is the carrying capacity, and \(W_1\) decreases as \(W_0\) increases.
\(r\) is the stationary phase constant, and \(W_1\) equals \(W_0 + rt\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q10 - Comparing absolute and relative leaf growth rates

questiontext.text: Two leaves, P and Q, increase in surface area by \(5\text{ cm}^2\) over the same unit time. Leaf P increases from \(10\text{ cm}^2\) to \(15\text{ cm}^2\), while Leaf Q increases from \(100\text{ cm}^2\) to \(105\text{ cm}^2\). Which statement correctly compares their relative growth rates (RGR)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Leaf P: \(A_{P,0} = 10\text{ cm}^2\), \(A_{P,1} = 15\text{ cm}^2\).
Leaf Q: \(A_{Q,0} = 100\text{ cm}^2\), \(A_{Q,1} = 105\text{ cm}^2\).
Time \(t = 1\text{ unit}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both leaves are measured under identical environmental conditions over the same unit time interval.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{AGR} = \frac{A_1 - A_0}{t}\) and \(\text{RGR} = \frac{A_1 - A_0}{A_0 \times t} \times 100\%\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For both leaves, \(\text{AGR} = 5\text{ cm}^2\text{ per unit time}\).
For Leaf P: \(\text{RGR}_P = \frac{5}{10} \times 100\% = 50\%\).
For Leaf Q: \(\text{RGR}_Q = \frac{5}{100} \times 100\% = 5\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Although both leaves have the same absolute growth rate (\(5\text{ cm}^2\)), Leaf P has a ten-fold higher relative growth rate (\(50\%\)) than Leaf Q (\(5\%\)).

answer.text: Both leaves have the same relative growth rate of \(5\%\).
Leaf P has a relative growth rate of \(50\%\), whereas Leaf Q has a relative growth rate of \(5\%\).
Leaf Q has a higher relative growth rate because its final area is larger.
Leaf P has a relative growth rate of \(150\%\), whereas Leaf Q has \(105\%\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q11 - Role of water in plant cell growth

questiontext.text: Why is plant growth and further development intimately linked to the water status of the plant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water, oxygen, and nutrients are essential conditions for plant growth.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plant cells grow in size by cell enlargement, which requires water so that turgidity of cells helps in extension growth. In addition, water provides the aqueous medium necessary for enzymatic activities needed for growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Water is essential because cell turgidity drives extension growth and it provides the medium for enzymatic activities.

answer.text: Water directly supplies carbon skeletons for protoplasm synthesis.
Water replaces oxygen in releasing metabolic energy for mitosis.
Turgidity of cells helps in extension growth and water provides the medium for enzymatic activities.
Water prevents cell wall deposition during the phase of elongation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q12 - Essential extrinsic factors for plant growth

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs an essential condition for plant growth with its primary role?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Growth requires water, oxygen, macro- and micro-nutrients, an optimum temperature range, and environmental signals like light and gravity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Oxygen helps in releasing metabolic energy essential for growth activities. Nutrients are required for synthesising protoplasm and acting as an energy source. Any deviation from the optimum temperature range can be detrimental to survival.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Oxygen helps in releasing metabolic energy essential for growth activities.

answer.text: Nutrients: provide turgidity for cell extension
Gravity: synthesises protoplasm directly
Optimum temperature: acts as a direct source of carbon
Oxygen: helps in releasing metabolic energy essential for growth activities

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q13 - Structural changes in tracheary element differentiation

questiontext.text: During differentiation to form a tracheary element, what major structural changes occur in the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Differentiation involves structural changes in both cell walls and protoplasm so that cells mature to perform specialised functions.

Step 2: Evaluation
To form a tracheary element, cells lose their protoplasm and develop very strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls. This enables them to carry water over long distances even under extreme tension.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Tracheary element differentiation involves loss of protoplasm and development of strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls.

answer.text: Loss of protoplasm and development of strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls
Increase in protoplasmic volume and thinning of primary cellulosic walls
Enlargement of the nucleus and formation of abundant plasmodesmata
Retention of dense cytoplasm and deposition of suberin without lignin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q14 - Dedifferentiation examples in higher plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of dedifferentiation in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dedifferentiation is the phenomenon in which living differentiated cells that have lost the capacity to divide regain the capacity of cell division under certain conditions.

Step 2: Evaluation
The formation of secondary meristems such as interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from fully differentiated parenchyma cells is a classic example of dedifferentiation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from fully differentiated parenchyma cells represents dedifferentiation.

answer.text: Maturation of root apical meristem derivatives into root-cap cells
Formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from fully differentiated parenchyma cells
Formation of tracheary elements directly from shoot apical meristem
Senescence and abscission of mature leaves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q15 - Products of redifferentiation in woody dicots

questiontext.text: When cells produced by dedifferentiated meristems such as vascular cambium or cork cambium once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions, the phenomenon is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant cells can undergo cycles of losing and regaining mitotic capacity during primary and secondary development.

Step 2: Evaluation
Meristems formed by dedifferentiation (such as interfascicular cambium and cork cambium) divide to produce new cells. When these daughter cells once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions (e.g., secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork), they are said to get redifferentiated.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This process is termed redifferentiation.

answer.text: Primary differentiation
Dedifferentiation
Redifferentiation
Plasticity

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q16 - Open differentiation and positional cell fate

questiontext.text: Why is differentiation in higher plants described as "open"?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Just as plant growth is open, differentiation in plants is also open rather than rigidly fixed at division.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cells and tissues arising out of the same meristem can have different structures at maturity. The final structure at maturity of a cell or tissue is determined by the location of the cell within the organ—for instance, cells positioned away from root apical meristems differentiate as root-cap cells, whereas those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Differentiation is open because cells arising from the same meristem acquire different mature structures depending on their location within the organ.

answer.text: Because all plant cells retain the ability to divide indefinitely without maturing
Because only dead cells can undergo differentiation
Because differentiated cells never undergo any structural changes in their cell walls
Because cells arising from the same meristem have different structures at maturity determined by their location

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q17 - Plasticity and juvenile versus adult heterophylly

questiontext.text: In which group of plants do leaves of the juvenile plant differ in shape from those in mature plants as an example of developmental plasticity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plasticity is the ability of plants to follow different pathways in response to the environment or phases of life to form different kinds of structures.

Step 2: Evaluation
Heterophylly between juvenile and mature plants is observed in cotton, coriander, and larkspur. In contrast, buttercup exhibits heterophylly due to environmental differences (air versus water).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cotton, coriander, and larkspur show heterophylly between juvenile and mature life phases.

answer.text: Cotton, coriander, and larkspur
Wheat, barley, and rye
Sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots
Buttercup, maize, and watermelon

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q18 - Environmental heterophylly in buttercup

questiontext.text: The difference in shapes of leaves produced in air versus those produced in water in buttercup illustrates:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants can modify their developmental pathways in response to external environmental conditions.

Step 2: Evaluation
In buttercup, leaves formed in terrestrial (air) habitat have a different shape from those formed in aquatic (water) habitat. This environmentally induced heterophylly is an example of plasticity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
It illustrates heterophyllous development due to environment, which is an example of plasticity.

answer.text: Apical dominance
Plasticity (heterophyllous development due to environment)
Vernalisation
Respiratory climactic

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q19 - Intrinsic and extrinsic factors in plant development

questiontext.text: Development in plants is controlled by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Which of the following correctly classifies an intracellular intrinsic factor and an intercellular intrinsic factor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Factors controlling plant growth and differentiation are classified as intrinsic (internal to the plant) and extrinsic (external to the plant).

Step 2: Evaluation
Intrinsic factors include both intracellular (genetic) factors and intercellular factors (chemicals such as plant growth regulators). Extrinsic factors include light, temperature, water, oxygen, and nutrition.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Genetic factors are intracellular intrinsic factors, while plant growth regulators are intercellular intrinsic factors.

answer.text: Intracellular: light; Intercellular: temperature
Intracellular: plant growth regulators; Intercellular: nutrition
Intracellular: genetic factors; Intercellular: plant growth regulators
Intracellular: water; Intercellular: oxygen

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q20 - Classification of plant growth promoters and inhibitors

questiontext.text: Which plant growth regulator could fit into either the growth-promoting or growth-inhibiting group, though it is largely an inhibitor of growth activities?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Based on their functions in a living plant body, PGRs are broadly divided into plant growth promoters (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins) and growth inhibitors.

Step 2: Evaluation
Abscisic acid belongs to the growth-inhibiting group (involved in dormancy, abscission, and stress responses). The gaseous PGR, ethylene, could fit either of the groups, but it is largely an inhibitor of growth activities.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ethylene is the gaseous PGR that could fit either group but is largely an inhibitor of growth activities.

answer.text: Gibberellic acid
Indole-3-acetic acid
Kinetin
Ethylene

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q21 - Chemical composition of kinetin and ABA

questiontext.text: Chemically, \(N^6\)-furfurylamino purine (kinetin) and abscisic acid (ABA) are respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The five major groups of PGRs are small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(N^6\)-furfurylamino purine (kinetin) is an adenine derivative, while abscisic acid (ABA) is a derivative of carotenoids. Indole-3-acetic acid is an indole compound, gibberellic acid is a terpene, and ethylene is a gas.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Kinetin is an adenine derivative and abscisic acid is a derivative of carotenoids.

answer.text: An adenine derivative and a derivative of carotenoids
An indole compound and a terpene
A terpene and an indole compound
A carotenoid derivative and a gaseous hydrocarbon

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q22 - Discovery of auxin from coleoptile tips

questiontext.text: Who first observed phototropism in coleoptiles of canary grass, and who later isolated auxin from the tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The discovery of auxins began with experiments on phototropism in grass coleoptiles.

Step 2: Evaluation
Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin observed that canary grass coleoptiles bent toward unilateral light and concluded that the coleoptile tip was the site of a transmittable influence. Later, F.W. Went isolated auxin from the tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin observed phototropism in canary grass, and F.W. Went isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips.

answer.text: F.W. Went; Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin
Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin; F.W. Went
E. Kurosawa; F. Skoog
Miller et al.; H.H. Cousins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q23 - Discovery of gibberellic acid in rice seedlings

questiontext.text: The 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease of rice seedlings, which led to the discovery of gibberellic acid, was caused by which fungal pathogen and studied using sterile filtrates by whom?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gibberellins were discovered accidentally while investigating an abnormal elongation disease in rice seedlings.

Step 2: Evaluation
The 'bakanae' disease of rice seedlings is caused by the fungal pathogen Gibberella fujikuroi. In 1926, E. Kurosawa reported that rice seedlings developed symptoms of this disease when treated with sterile filtrates of the fungus, and the active substances were later identified as gibberellic acid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pathogen is Gibberella fujikuroi and the researcher who used sterile filtrates was E. Kurosawa.

answer.text: Penicillium notatum; F.W. Went
Rhizopus stolonifer; H.H. Cousins
Gibberella fujikuroi; E. Kurosawa
Aspergillus niger; F. Skoog

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q24 - Discovery of kinetin from tobacco callus

questiontext.text: F. Skoog and his co-workers observed that callus from internodal segments of tobacco stems proliferated only when auxin in the nutrient medium was supplemented with certain extracts. Which set of supplements supported this proliferation, leading Miller et al. (1955) to crystallise kinetin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cytokinins were discovered during plant tissue culture studies investigating the factors required for cytokinesis and callus proliferation.

Step 2: Evaluation
F. Skoog and co-workers found that tobacco stem internodal callus proliferated only if, in addition to auxins, the nutrient medium was supplemented with one of the following: extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk, or DNA. Miller et al. (1955) later identified and crystallised the cytokinesis-promoting substance and termed it kinetin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk, or DNA supplemented with auxin supported callus proliferation.

answer.text: Abscisic acid, phenolic acids, or nitrates
Sterile filtrates of Gibberella fujikuroi or ethylene gas
2,4-D, ethephon, or para-ascorbic acid
Extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk, or DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q25 - Discovery of abscisic acid from three inhibitors

questiontext.text: During the mid-1960s, three independent researches purified and characterised three inhibitors that were later proved to be chemically identical and named abscisic acid (ABA). What were those three inhibitors?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abscisic acid was independently discovered by researchers studying growth inhibition, abscission, and dormancy.

Step 2: Evaluation
The three independently characterised inhibitors that proved to be chemically identical and were named abscisic acid (ABA) were inhibitor-B, abscission II, and dormin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Inhibitor-B, abscission II, and dormin were proved chemically identical and named abscisic acid.

answer.text: Inhibitor-B, abscission II, and dormin
Zeatin, kinetin, and ethephon
Inhibitor-A, vernalin, and florigen
Phenolic acid, para-ascorbic acid, and IBA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q26 - Natural versus synthetic auxins

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs consists exclusively of synthetic auxins?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Auxins include both naturally occurring plant compounds and synthetic compounds with auxin-like growth-regulating properties.

Step 2: Evaluation
IAA (indole-3-acetic acid) and IBA (indole butyric acid) are natural auxins isolated from plants. NAA (naphthalene acetic acid) and 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) are synthetic auxins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
NAA and 2,4-D are exclusively synthetic auxins.

answer.text: IAA and IBA
NAA and 2,4-D
IAA and NAA
IBA and zeatin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q27 - Auxin role in abscission and parthenocarpy

questiontext.text: How do auxins affect leaf and fruit drop at different stages of maturity, and what effect do they have on tomatoes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Auxins regulate abscission depending on the developmental stage of leaves and fruits, and also influence fruit development without fertilisation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Auxins help prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages, but promote the abscission of older mature leaves and fruits. They also induce parthenocarpy, for example in tomatoes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Auxins prevent early fruit and leaf drop, promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits, and induce parthenocarpy in tomatoes.

answer.text: Promote early drop; prevent abscission of older leaves; delay ripening in tomatoes
Prevent abscission at all stages; induce bolting in tomatoes
Prevent drop at early stages; promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits; induce parthenocarpy in tomatoes
Promote drop of young leaves only; induce seed dormancy in tomatoes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q28 - Apical dominance and decapitation in horticulture

questiontext.text: Why is decapitation (removal of shoot tips) widely practised in tea plantations and hedge-making?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In most higher plants, the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of lateral (axillary) buds, a phenomenon called apical dominance.

Step 2: Evaluation
Removing the shoot tip (decapitation) eliminates the source of apical dominance, resulting in the growth of lateral buds into branches. This produces bushier tea plants with more pluckable shoots and denser hedges.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Decapitation removes apical dominance and promotes the growth of lateral buds.

answer.text: To induce parthenocarpy in lateral flowers
To promote vertical elongation of the main stem
To trigger stomatal closure and reduce transpiration
To overcome apical dominance and promote the growth of lateral buds

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q29 - Selective herbicidal action of 2,4-D

questiontext.text: A gardener sprays a lawn with 2,4-D to make it weed-free. Which of the following explains why this treatment is effective without harming the lawn grass?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D are widely used as selective herbicides in agriculture and horticulture.

Step 2: Evaluation
2,4-D selectively kills dicotyledonous weeds while not affecting mature monocotyledonous plants (such as lawn grasses). Additionally, auxins control xylem differentiation and help in cell division.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
2,4-D kills dicotyledonous weeds without affecting mature monocotyledonous lawn grasses.

answer.text: 2,4-D kills dicotyledonous weeds but does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants.
2,4-D kills monocotyledonous weeds while stimulating dicotyledonous grasses.
2,4-D inhibits xylem differentiation exclusively in monocotyledonous stems.
2,4-D acts as an antagonist to natural auxins in grass roots.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q30 - Physiological effects of gibberellins on fruits

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT a physiological effect of gibberellins?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gibberellins are acidic, promotory PGRs with over 100 known forms (\(\text{GA}_1, \text{GA}_2, \text{GA}_3\), etc.).

Step 2: Evaluation
Gibberellins increase the length of grape stalks, cause fruits like apple to elongate and improve shape, and delay senescence so fruits can stay on the tree longer to extend the market period. Promoting abscission and senescence of leaves and flowers is a function of ethylene, not gibberellins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Promoting senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers is not a physiological effect of gibberellins.

answer.text: Increasing the length of grape stalks
Promoting senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers
Causing fruits like apple to elongate and improve their shape
Delaying senescence to extend the market period of fruits on the tree

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q31 - Agricultural and industrial uses of gibberellins

questiontext.text: How does spraying juvenile conifers with gibberellins benefit forestry, and what effect does it have on rosette plants like beet and cabbage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gibberellins promote stem axis elongation and accelerate developmental transitions in several plant species.

Step 2: Evaluation
Spraying juvenile conifers with gibberellins hastens the maturity period, leading to early seed production. In beet, cabbages, and many plants with a rosette habit, gibberellins promote bolting (internode elongation just prior to flowering).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Gibberellins hasten maturity for early seed production in juvenile conifers and promote bolting in rosette plants.

answer.text: Delays seed production in conifers; induces stomatal closure in rosette plants
Induces dormancy in conifers; suppresses flowering in rosette plants
Hastens maturity for early seed production in conifers; promotes bolting in rosette plants
Promotes root hair formation in conifers; inhibits internode elongation in rosette plants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q32 - Natural versus synthetic cytokinins zeatin kinetin

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately distinguishes kinetin from zeatin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cytokinins have specific effects on cytokinesis and include both naturally occurring plant substances and synthetic or non-plant derivatives.

Step 2: Evaluation
Kinetin was discovered from autoclaved herring sperm DNA and does not occur naturally in plants. Zeatin is a naturally occurring cytokinin isolated from corn-kernels and coconut milk.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Kinetin does not occur naturally in plants, whereas zeatin is a natural cytokinin isolated from corn-kernels and coconut milk.

answer.text: Kinetin is isolated from corn-kernels, whereas zeatin is isolated from herring sperm DNA.
Both kinetin and zeatin occur naturally in all higher plants.
Zeatin is a terpene derivative, whereas kinetin is an indole compound.
Kinetin does not occur naturally in plants, whereas zeatin is a natural cytokinin isolated from corn-kernels and coconut milk.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q33 - Synthesis sites and physiological roles of cytokinins

questiontext.text: Where are natural cytokinins synthesised in plants, and how do they delay leaf senescence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Natural cytokinins are associated with regions of active cell division and shoot development.

Step 2: Evaluation
Natural cytokinins are synthesised in regions where rapid cell division occurs, such as root apices, developing shoot buds, and young fruits. They help produce new leaves, chloroplasts in leaves, lateral shoot growth, and adventitious shoot formation. They delay leaf senescence by promoting nutrient mobilisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Natural cytokinins are synthesised in regions of rapid cell division and delay leaf senescence by promoting nutrient mobilisation.

answer.text: Synthesised in regions of rapid cell division (root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits); delay senescence by promoting nutrient mobilisation
Synthesised only in senescent leaves; delay senescence by closing stomata
Synthesised in mature xylem vessels; delay senescence by inducing apical dominance
Synthesised in dormant seeds; delay senescence by inhibiting chloroplast formation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q34 - Ethylene synthesis and respiratory climactic

questiontext.text: What is "respiratory climactic" in plant physiology, and which plant growth regulator causes it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR synthesised in large amounts by tissues undergoing senescence and ripening fruits.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ethylene is highly effective in fruit ripening and enhances the rate of respiration during the ripening of fruits. This characteristic rise in respiration rate is called respiratory climactic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Respiratory climactic is the rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening, caused by ethylene.

answer.text: Decrease in respiration during seed germination, caused by abscisic acid
Rise in the rate of respiration during fruit ripening, caused by ethylene
Increase in photosynthesis during flowering, caused by gibberellins
Rapid stomatal opening under drought, caused by cytokinins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q35 - Diverse physiological effects of ethylene

questiontext.text: Which combination of physiological responses is promoted by ethylene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethylene regulates numerous physiological processes across seedlings, roots, tubers, seeds, and submerged plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ethylene induces horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis, and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings. It breaks seed and bud dormancy (initiating germination in peanut seeds and sprouting of potato tubers), promotes rapid internode/petiole elongation in deep water rice, and promotes root growth and root hair formation to increase absorption surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Apical hook formation in dicot seedlings, sprouting of potato tubers, and root hair formation are all promoted by ethylene.

answer.text: Apical dominance, parthenocarpy in tomatoes, and stomatal closure
Bolting in cabbages, delay of leaf senescence, and malting in brewing
Apical hook formation in dicot seedlings, sprouting of potato tubers, and root hair formation
Seed dormancy maintenance, chloroplast synthesis, and weed-free lawns

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q36 - Agricultural applications of ethephon

questiontext.text: Ethephon is the most widely used compound as a source of ethylene in agriculture. Which of the following accurately describes its properties and uses?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethephon is an aqueous compound that is readily absorbed and transported within the plant, where it releases ethylene slowly.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ethephon hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples, accelerates abscission in flowers and fruits (used for thinning of cotton, cherry, and walnut), and promotes female flowers in cucumbers thereby increasing yield.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ethephon releases ethylene slowly in aqueous solution, hastens ripening in tomatoes and apples, thins cotton/cherry/walnut, and promotes female flowers in cucumbers.

answer.text: It releases gibberellin slowly and prevents fruit abscission in cotton and walnut.
It is insoluble in water and promotes male flowers in cucumbers.
It delays fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples to extend market period.
It is readily absorbed in aqueous solution, releases ethylene slowly, accelerates fruit thinning in cotton/cherry/walnut, and promotes female flowers in cucumbers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q37 - Abscisic acid as the stress hormone

questiontext.text: Why is abscisic acid (ABA) also called the "stress hormone" in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
ABA acts as a general plant growth inhibitor and an inhibitor of plant metabolism, playing a key role in plant responses to stress.

Step 2: Evaluation
ABA stimulates the closure of stomata and increases the tolerance of plants to various kinds of biotic and abiotic stresses. Therefore, it is referred to as the stress hormone.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ABA is called the stress hormone because it stimulates stomatal closure and increases plant tolerance to various stresses.

answer.text: It stimulates the closure of stomata and increases plant tolerance to various kinds of stresses.
It promotes rapid internode elongation when plants are submerged in water.
It breaks seed dormancy during cold winter temperatures.
It increases nutrient mobilisation to prevent leaf senescence under drought.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q38 - ABA antagonism to GAs in seed dormancy

questiontext.text: In seed development, maturation, and dormancy, how does abscisic acid (ABA) help seeds survive unfavourable conditions, and which PGR does it typically antagonise?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
More than one PGR often interacts to regulate key developmental events such as seed dormancy, with some PGRs acting antagonistically.

Step 2: Evaluation
ABA plays an important role in seed development, maturation, and dormancy. By inducing dormancy, ABA helps seeds withstand desiccation and other factors unfavourable for growth. In most situations, ABA acts as an antagonist to gibberellins (GAs), which promote germination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ABA induces dormancy to help seeds withstand desiccation and acts as an antagonist to gibberellins (GAs).

answer.text: By promoting rapid germination; acts synergistically with auxins
By inducing dormancy to withstand desiccation; acts as an antagonist to gibberellins (GAs)
By breaking hard seed coats; acts as an antagonist to ethylene
By stimulating cell division in embryos; acts synergistically with gibberellins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q39 - Effect of omitting cytokinin or mixing rotten fruit

questiontext.text: What would be expected to happen if a rotten fruit gets mixed with unripe fruits in storage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ripening fruits and senescing tissues produce large amounts of the gaseous PGR ethylene.

Step 2: Evaluation
A rotten (over-ripe) fruit releases ethylene gas, which diffuses to the surrounding unripe fruits, enhances their respiration rate (respiratory climactic), and hastens their ripening.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The unripe fruits will ripen faster due to ethylene released by the rotten fruit.

answer.text: The unripe fruits will remain dormant indefinitely due to ABA release.
The unripe fruits will elongate rapidly due to gibberellin release.
The unripe fruits will ripen faster due to ethylene released by the rotten fruit.
The unripe fruits will delay senescence due to cytokinin release.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q40 - Consequence of dividing cells failing to differentiate

questiontext.text: What would happen in a plant if actively dividing meristematic cells completely stopped differentiating, or if cytokinin was omitted from a tobacco stem callus culture medium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal plant development requires both cell division (growth) and cell specialisation (differentiation). In tissue culture, callus proliferation requires both auxins and cytokinins.

Step 2: Evaluation
If dividing cells stop differentiating, they continue dividing without forming specialised tissues or organs, resulting in an unorganised mass of cells (callus or tumour-like growth). Similarly, if cytokinin is omitted from a culture medium containing only auxin, callus proliferation and cytokinesis will not occur properly.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Failure of dividing cells to differentiate results in an unorganised mass of cells rather than organised tissues and organs, and omitting cytokinin prevents proper callus proliferation.

answer.text: Organised vascular tissues will form faster; callus will proliferate vigorously without cytokinin.
Cells will immediately enter seed dormancy; callus will form roots and shoots rapidly.
Tracheary elements will form without wall thickening; callus will bolt.
An unorganised mass of cells will form without specialised tissues/organs; callus will fail to proliferate properly without cytokinin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q41 - Classification of plants by photoperiodic response

questiontext.text: In photoperiodism, how are long day plants, short day plants, and day-neutral plants distinguished, and what is the role of the dark period?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Photoperiodism is the flowering response of plants to periodic exposures of light and dark durations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Long day plants require exposure to light for a period exceeding a well-defined critical duration, short day plants must be exposed to light for a period less than this critical duration, and day-neutral plants show no correlation between light duration and flowering. Furthermore, the duration of the dark period is of equal importance as the light period.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Flowering depends on the relative durations of both light and dark periods, with long day plants flowering above the critical duration, short day plants below it, and day-neutral plants showing no such correlation.

answer.text: Long day plants flower above critical light duration, short day plants below it, day-neutral plants show no correlation; dark period is equally important.
Long day plants require less than 12 hours of light, short day plants require more than 12 hours; dark period has no effect.
All three plant groups have the exact same critical duration; only light intensity matters.
Day-neutral plants flower only in complete darkness; long day plants flower only in continuous light.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q42 - Simultaneous flowering of short and long day plants

questiontext.text: How can both a short day plant and a long day plant flower simultaneously at the same place under identical day-length conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The critical photoperiodic duration is not a fixed universal number; it differs for different plant species.

Step 2: Evaluation
If a long day plant has a critical duration of, for example, \(10\text{ hours}\) and a short day plant has a critical duration of \(14\text{ hours}\), then a \(12\text{-hour}\) day length exceeds the critical duration of the long day plant while remaining below the critical duration of the short day plant. Thus, both can flower simultaneously.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They can flower simultaneously because critical duration varies among species, so a given day length can be above the critical duration for the long day plant and below it for the short day plant.

answer.text: Because both plants convert into day-neutral plants when grown together
Because critical duration differs for different plants, so the same day length can exceed the critical duration of the long day plant while being below that of the short day plant
Because shoot apices perceive light independently of leaves in mixed cultures
Because vernalisation eliminates photoperiodic requirements in all plants

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q43 - Effect of defoliation on photoperiodic flowering

questiontext.text: Would a completely defoliated plant respond to an inductive photoperiodic cycle to initiate flowering?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although shoot apices modify themselves into flowering apices prior to flowering, they cannot perceive photoperiods by themselves.

Step 2: Evaluation
The site of perception of light and dark durations is the leaves. When exposed to the necessary inductive photoperiod, a hypothesised hormonal substance migrates from the leaves to the shoot apices to induce flowering. Without leaves, the plant cannot perceive the photoperiodic cycle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
No, a defoliated plant will not respond to a photoperiodic cycle because leaves are the site of perception of light and dark durations.

answer.text: Yes, because shoot apices directly perceive light and dark durations.
Yes, because roots synthesise the flowering hormone upon illumination.
No, because leaves are the site of perception of light and dark durations.
No, because defoliation permanently destroys the shoot apical meristem.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q44 - Definition and significance of vernalisation

questiontext.text: What is vernalisation, and what is its primary developmental significance in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain plants depend quantitatively or qualitatively on exposure to low temperature to initiate flowering later in life.

Step 2: Evaluation
Vernalisation refers specially to the promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature. It prevents precocious reproductive development late in the growing season and enables the plant to have sufficient time to reach maturity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by low temperature, preventing precocious reproductive development late in the growing season.

answer.text: Promotion of seed dormancy by high temperature to prevent germination
Promotion of leaf abscission by short day lengths in autumn
Induction of parthenocarpy by auxin spray during summer
Promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature, preventing precocious reproductive development late in the growing season

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q45 - Winter and spring varieties of cereal crops

questiontext.text: In wheat, barley, and rye, why are "winter" varieties planted in autumn rather than in spring?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Wheat, barley, and rye have two varieties—spring and winter—differing in their vernalisation requirement.

Step 2: Evaluation
Spring varieties are planted in spring and flower and produce grain before the end of the growing season. Winter varieties, if planted in spring, normally fail to flower or produce mature grain within a single flowering season because they require a cold period (vernalisation). Therefore, they are planted in autumn, overwinter as small seedlings, resume growth in spring, and are harvested around mid-summer.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Winter varieties are planted in autumn so they receive winter cold (vernalisation) as seedlings; if planted in spring, they fail to flower or produce mature grain within that season.

answer.text: Because if planted in spring, they fail to flower or produce mature grain within a single flowering season
Because their seeds cannot germinate at temperatures above \(10^{\circ}\text{C}\)
Because they are biennial plants that always die after the first winter
Because they are short day plants that flower only in December

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q46 - Vernalisation response in biennial plants

questiontext.text: Which group represents monocarpic biennial plants in which cold treatment stimulates a subsequent photoperiodic flowering response?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biennials are monocarpic plants that normally flower and die in their second growing season.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots are common biennial plants. Subjecting a growing biennial plant to a cold treatment (vernalisation) stimulates a subsequent photoperiodic flowering response.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots are monocarpic biennials exhibiting vernalisation.

answer.text: Cotton, coriander, and larkspur
Sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots
Pineapple, mango, and cucumber
Tomato, apple, and cherry

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q47 - Endogenous causes of seed dormancy

questiontext.text: Which of the following are endogenous factors that cause seed dormancy even when external environmental conditions are favourable?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seed dormancy is controlled not by the external environment, but by endogenous conditions within the seed itself.

Step 2: Evaluation
Endogenous causes of seed dormancy include: (1) an impermeable and hard seed coat, (2) presence of chemical inhibitors such as abscisic acid, phenolic acids, and para-ascorbic acid, and (3) immature embryos.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hard impermeable seed coats, chemical inhibitors (abscisic acid, phenolic acids, para-ascorbic acid), and immature embryos cause endogenous seed dormancy.

answer.text: Presence of gibberellic acid, nitrates, and abundant oxygen
Thin cellulosic seed coat and excess cytokinin levels
Impermeable hard seed coat, chemical inhibitors (abscisic acid, phenolic acids, para-ascorbic acid), and immature embryos
Lack of water, low oxygen availability, and suboptimal temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MCQ_Q48 - Natural and artificial methods to break seed dormancy

questiontext.text: How can seed dormancy caused by an impermeable seed coat versus chemical inhibitors be overcome?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seed dormancy can be broken by natural means or man-made measures targeting the specific endogenous barrier.

Step 2: Evaluation
A hard seed coat barrier can be broken by mechanical abrasions using knives, sandpaper, or vigorous shaking (or naturally by microbial action and passage through the digestive tract of animals). The effect of inhibitory substances can be removed by subjecting seeds to chilling conditions or applying chemicals such as gibberellic acid and nitrates, as well as changing light and temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Seed coat barriers are overcome by mechanical or natural abrasions, while chemical inhibitors are overcome by chilling conditions or applying gibberellic acid and nitrates.

answer.text: Seed coat barrier: abscisic acid application; inhibitors: mechanical shaking
Seed coat barrier: chilling conditions; inhibitors: passage through animal digestive tract
Seed coat barrier: phenolic acid spray; inhibitors: knives and sandpaper
Seed coat barrier: mechanical or natural abrasions (microbial action / animal digestive tract); inhibitors: chilling or applying gibberellic acid and nitrates
